title: TA9-08613
frame:
Forum: Refugee Protection Division (first-instance tribunal).
Parties: the claimant and the Minister; names are redacted.
Decision under review: none; this is the first-instance decision.
How the layers nest here: The member of the tribunal is the author (layer 1). The claimant and the Minister make submissions to the member (layer 2). There is no earlier decision-maker unless the reasons describe a prior decision (layer 3). Testimony and documents are layer 5.

paragraphs.text: The claimants, XXXXXX ("XXXX"), his common-law spouse, XXXXXXXX ("XXXX"), their minor children, XXXXX ("XXX"), XXXXXX ("XXXX"), XXXXXXXX ("XXXX") and XXXXXXXXX ("XXXX"), and XXXX's adult son from a previous relationship, XXXXXXX ("XXXX"), citizens of the Czech Republic, seek refugee protection pursuant to sections 96 and 97(1) of the Immigration and Refugee Protection Act1 (IRPA). The claimants' identities have been established through identity documents filed in evidence.2
These claims were joined according to Rule 49(1) of the Refugee Protection Division Rules. XXXX was appointed as the designated representative for the minor claimants, XXX, XXXXX, XXXX and XXXX.
The claims of XXXX's sons, XXXXXXX ("XXXX") and XXXXXXX ("XXXX"), were withdrawn prior to the hearing.

The claimants' fears are based on their Romani ethnicity. They maintain that they experienced discrimination, harassment and abuse in many areas of life in the Czech Republic, including education, employment and health care.
The following is a summary of the claimants' allegations:

XXXX was ignored by his teachers at school. At twelve years of age, he was diagnosed with an untreatable medical condition that caused him XXXX. Bigger students would call him names and kick and throw him to the ground. After XXXX finished elementary school, he could not obtain immediate employment because he was disabled and Roma. He spent two years without a job; part of that time was spent in hospital recovering from his medical condition.

In 2000, skinheads marched along the streets of XXXX. They shouted racist and anti-Roma slogans and threw bricks at the houses of the Roma. In 2002, three skinheads chased XXXX from the train station where he was waiting for a train.

In 2006, while pregnant with XXXX, XXXX was rushed to hospital in an ambulance due to bleeding. While in her hospital room, XXXX began to have contractions and called for assistance but no one came. XXXX left her room to obtain assistance and was attended to by a nurse. The nurse offered little assistance and dislocated the baby's shoulder while delivering her. XXXX was born with bruises and was blue from lack of oxygen.

XXXX was called names at school and teachers did not do anything about it. He began missing school and having problems and was eventually placed in a foster home. While in foster care, XXXX attended a XXXX school to become XXXX. XXXX was physically assaulted by friends of a skinhead he went to school with. XXXX was mistreated at the foster home and would occasionally run away. On one occasion, XXXX was humiliated by a group of skinheads who told him to kneel down in the middle of the road and declare that the country was theirs.
Starting in 2007, while attending XXXX school for XXXXXX, XXXX was regularly called names and physically assaulted by ethnic Czech students.
In XXXXX 2008, XXXX was attacked by a group of skinheads who took his cane and used it to physically assault him. The skinheads also assaulted XXXX.

In XXXX 2009, XXXX was physically assaulted by four skinheads as she was making her way home. XXXX called police and ambulance but neither arrived before XXXX picked her up to take her to the doctor and police station.
In 2009, four neo-Nazis physically assaulted XXXX.
The claimants fled the Czech Republic on XXXX, 2009 and filed claims for refugee protection in Canada the same day.
I find that the claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. ANALYSIS Determinative Issues
The determinative issue in these claims is state protection. State Protection

There is a presumption that a state is capable of protecting its citizens. The claimants may rebut this presumption by providing "clear and convincing" proof of lack of state protection. The claimants must approach the state for protection, providing state protection might be reasonably forthcoming.3 Evidence that protection being offered is not necessarily perfect4 is not clear and convincing proof of the state's inability to protect its citizens, as no government can guarantee the protection of all its citizens at all times. However, where a state is in effective control of its territory, has military, police and civil authorities in place and makes serious efforts to protect its citizens, the mere fact it is not always successful at doing so will not be enough to justify that the claimants are unable to avail themselves of protection.5

When the state in question is a democratic state, the claimants must do more than simply show that they approached a member of a police force and that their efforts were unsuccessful. The burden for the claimants is to prove an absence of state protection that is directly proportional to the level of democracy of that state.6 The more democratic the state's institutions, the greater the onus is on the claimants to show that they have exhausted all courses of action available.7 Moreover, local failures by the authorities to provide protection do not mean that the state as a whole fails to protect its citizens, unless the failures form part of a broader pattern of state inability or refusal to provide protection.8

The documentary evidence shows that Czech Republic is a functioning, parliamentary democracy with free and fair elections.9 I find that Czech Republic is in effective control of its territory and has in place a functioning security force to uphold the laws and constitution of the country. There is nothing in the documentation before the Board to suggest that the Czech Republic is in a state of complete breakdown.

In view of the above noted principles, I find that the claimants have not provided clear and convincing evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, state protection in the Czech Republic is inadequate. In this particular case, XXXX, XXXX and XXXX were questioned with respect to state protection in Czech Republic.

XXXX testified that, right after the XXXXXX 2008 incident, two police cars arrived. He went on to say that bystanders had called police. After police arrived, they first asked XXXX and XXXX if they needed medical attention and began asking witnesses about the incident. Police took XXXX and XXXX to a place with doctors where x-rays were taken. They had bruises and scratches; XXXX had hair missing; and XXXX's cane was broken. Police then drove XXXX and XXXX to XXXX mother's house. The following day police returned to pick up XXXX and XXXX and took them to the police station. Police wrote a report and took the victims' official statements regarding how the incident happened. Police told XXXX and XXXX that they would work on it. XXXX returned to the police station 14 days later and was told that there was nothing new. XXXX told police that they made a mistake in trying to solve the case and asked them to lift the assailants' fingerprints from his cane. He also asked police if they obtained any of the witnesses' statements and was told that the witnesses did not see anything except his assailants running away. XXXX returned to the police station three weeks later and was told that the case was still open. He realized that police were not going to do anything so he did not go back afterwards. XXXX indicated that he went to police often for various things and nothing ever came of them; even for regular things.

XXXX testified that XXXX was physically assaulted by four skinheads in XXXX on XXXX XX, 2009 at approximately 8:00 p.m. XXXX went on to say that XXXX returned home at approximately 10:00 p.m. and his leg and arm were hurting. XXXX took XXXX to the hospital in XXXX and then to the police station in XXXX at approximately 11:00 p.m. XXXX told police that he was attacked by skinheads. Police asked XXXX where and when he was attacked, what his assailants looked like and if he went to the doctor for medical treatment. XXXX told police that the skinheads were driving by wearing facemask; most of his friends took off; and he and two friends were attacked. Police told XXXX and XXXX that there was nothing they could do as XXXX and his two friends could not describe their attackers. Police asked XXXX and XXXX how they are expected to find XXXX's attackers if they do not know who to look for. XXXX testified that he and XXXX knew it was the skinheads from XXXX. The police officer told them he would make a phone call. XXXX believes that he may have called the XXXX police station. The police officer told XXXX and XXXX that police would let them know if they found out anything. XXXX also indicated that police were always driving around their building; that police knew him because he was always complaining to them and they would have told him if they found out anything about XXXX's attack.

XXXX testified that, after she was attacked in XXXX 2009, she went to a convenience store and told the female attendant that she was Roma and was beaten up by skinheads. The attendant gave XXXX a chair to sit on and called police. After asking XXXX if she needed an ambulance, to which XXXX responded that she did, the attendant also called for an ambulance. After waiting for an hour without the arrival of police or ambulance, XXXX called her husband who picked her up and drove her to the doctor. The doctor examined XXXX and prescribed her with medication for the pain in her ribs. XXXX then drove XXXX to police. Police wrote a report and took XXXX's statement. Police asked her what her assailants looked like but since the attack occurred at dawn (not in full daylight) and her assailants covered their faces, XXXX was unable to provide police with a description, stating that only the two female skinheads (and not the two male skinheads that accompanied them) had physically assaulted her. Police told XXXX that they would try to solve the crime and let her know. After two weeks, XXXX returned to the police station to ask if police were able to successfully investigate the incident. Police told XXXX that they did not know anything at that time and did not have any evidence or any leads to follow.

XXXX testified that after he was physically assaulted by a group of ethnic Czechs at the XXXX school he was attending, he was called to a meeting at the school. In attendance at the meeting were the police, the school principal and those who attacked him. Police wrote down everything that was said and he returned to class. XXXX went on to say that he had one more meeting with the principal after the meeting with police and his father wanted to ask the principal exactly what happened. The principal explained everything to XXXX and XXXX and told them that police knew about the physical assault against XXXX and that XXXX's assailants would get criminal records if it happened again. When asked if he was physical assaulted by the ethnic Hungarians at his XXXX school ever again, XXXX testified that it was just verbal or a push but his assailants were afraid to physically attack him after that.

I find that police acted appropriately to XXXX, XXXX and XXXX's complaints noted above. Police took their statements and questioned each of them regarding their allegations. Police told them they would look into the matter or investigate. Police cannot be expected to investigate all alleged crimes reported to them. They must assess the availability of evidence, their resources and the chances of successfully locating and possibly charging and prosecuting the perpetrators. Police cannot be expected to successfully investigate all crimes reported to them especially if the incident is not immediately reported, the identity of the perpetrator is unknown and an accurate description cannot be ascertained. This was the case for most of the incidents reported by XXXX and XXXX. Most of the incidents were reported well after they occurred. Accurate descriptions of the assailants were not available. Considering the time lapse between the incidents and when they were reported to police, the lack of an adequate description of the assailants and the fact that their location was unknown since the attacks occurred in public places and it was not known where the assailants traveled to, it is unlikely that police would be successful in identifying XXXX or XXXX's assailants or locating them. It is clear from their response to XXXX and XXXX allegations that police assessed the various factors noted above in determining whether to investigate any further or not.

It is unclear why police and ambulance did not respond or took a very long time to respond to the convenience store attendant's calls for assistance in the XXXX 2009 incident involving XXXX. Insufficient evidence was presented to indicate that police and ambulance did not respond to the calls whatsoever. If police and ambulance responded after XXXX left the scene, it is not known why it took them an inordinate amount of time to arrive. As such, a clear finding could not be determined regarding the police and ambulance response to the scene of the XXXX 2009 incident. However, the medical attention XXXX received after XXXX drove her to the doctor and the police response to XXXX's allegations after she reported them at the police station were appropriate.

When the incident regarding XXXX was reported to police and the identities of the perpetrators was known to the school and the police, the perpetrators were called to a meeting with school officials and police. The perpetrators were told that they would have criminal records if it happens again. XXXX was never physically assaulted by this group of individuals again. This demonstrates that police respond accordingly to accusations of physical assaults, even by ethnic Romani XXXX school students, and take appropriate and effective action, as evidenced by the cessation of physical assaults against XXXX by the group of ethnic Hungarians.

I find that the claimants have failed to rebut the presumption of state protection with clear and convincing evidence. No credible evidence was presented to indicate that police did not act appropriately to XXXX, XXXX or XXXX's allegations when they were notified. If they were dissatisfied with the response of police to their allegations, documentary evidence noted below indicates that recourse would be available to them. Insufficient credible evidence was presented to indicate that the claimants would not be helped if they sought the assistance of police for any other matter or sought redress through the mechanisms in place in the Czech Republic.

I am not persuaded that police did not investigate all of XXXX, XXXX and XXXX's allegations regarding the above noted incidents. I am also not persuaded that police would not investigate all of the claimants' allegations if they were reported in a timely manner and with sufficient detail and evidence for police to pursue. Recourse would be available to the claimants if police did not respond to their allegations. I am not persuaded that police would not prosecute all of the claimants' assailants if there was sufficient evidence. I found XXXX and XXXX's responses regarding the effectiveness of state protection were not persuasive, since they were largely unsubstantiated and not consistent with the documentary evidence. I find that the claimants did not prove that police in the Czech Republic would not investigate all of their allegations and prosecute the perpetrators if there was sufficient evidence. As such, the claimants have not provided clear and convincing evidence that, on a balance of probabilities, state protection in the Czech Republic is inadequate.

The documentary evidence indicates that the government generally respected and protected the rights of its citizens.10 While there is no question that Roma do face discrimination and that there have been demonstrations and even some attacks at the hands of skinheads, neo-Nazis and other extremists,11 there is legislation in place that provides protection for the Roma and other groups including anti-discrimination and hate-crime legislation. The Czech constitution prohibits discrimination based on national, racial or ethnic background as well as other pieces of legislation governing employment and education as well as The Charter of Rights and Freedoms. An anti-discrimination bill which would harmonize Czech legislation with that of the European Union was passed on June 17, 2009. Furthermore, the Czech Republic is a member of the European Union, which has had a positive impact on the country by setting standards concerning human rights, as well as access to the European Court of Human Rights and access to multi lateral programs such as the Decade of Roma Inclusion. I do note that some observers have questioned the degree of positive impact that these measures have had.12

To address acts of discrimination, the authorities introduced the Roma Police Assistant (RPA) program in 2003. The purpose of employing RPAs is to assist in building better relations and trust between the Roma and the police. The RPAs assist police in their investigations and assist in accompanying Roma who are victims of crime to file police reports and in obtaining social services for such victims. A program of hiring Minority Liason Officers (MLOs) was also begun in 2004 with the focus on crime reduction and lessening social exclusion. Several observers have commented that these programs have been helpful and represent progress in the relationship between Roma and the authorities, which has not been one of trust over the years. Furthermore, in the mid 1990s, the Ministry of the Interior initiated programs to combat extremists by allowing the police to closely monitor such group activities and created an anti-extremist department within the police itself, which is showing signs of success. The police have arrested neo-Nazis and they have been prosecuted, including a case where a Romani had been murdered. The police also successfully prevented or broke up extremist clashes and demonstrations. The government is trying to recruit Roma as police officers, with a number of drives being conducted in Prague and Brno. While there has been a good response to these drives, many applicants are screened out due to a lack of a secondary school diploma. However, to counter-act this problem, the police and other organizations offer assistance to people who want to complete their education so that they can then join the police force. Furthermore, the police are trained on how to deal with minorities and extremists. The police are making other efforts such as participating in day camps, seminars and school visits in order to foster better relations with Roma children. While statistics are difficult to come by given privacy laws, as of 2006, there were an estimated 61 Roma police officers in the Czech Republic.13

The judiciary has prosecuted hate crimes committed against Roma people on several occasions. The documentary evidence notes that "the judicial proceedings on racial crime have increased in recent years due to the efforts of NGOs ..."14 The Czech Ombudsman was created in 1999 and is known as the Public Defender of Rights. The Ombudsman investigates allegations of public sector mistreatment of Roma and may take corrective action or issue advice or recommendations. The Ombudsman has successfully intervened in areas such as housing but has yet to receive any formal complaints against the police.15 There are other government and non government agencies available to assist the Roma, including 400 Roma NGOs, the Czech Trade Inspectorate (to deal with unfair business practices or consumer discrimination), and the Social Inclusion Agency to address the social integration of the Roma into Czech society, including housing, health care, employment, social services and cohesion.16

The above noted evidence demonstrates that the Czech Republic has made significant efforts to provide better protection for all its citizens and especially the Roma in all areas of life such as education, health care and employment. The evidence also demonstrates that the Czech Republic is serious about curbing crime and corruption, including crimes committed against the Roma. The Czech Republic's successes in these endeavors are clearly noticeable in this documentation.

I have considered the documentary evidence submitted by counsel. The European Roma Rights Centre report Attacks against Roma in the Czech Republic: January 2008 - April 201117 documents 19 attacks against the Roma and their property in the Czech Republic between January 2008 and April 2011. Also documented is the police response to some of the attacks such as the arrest of the non-Romani neighbours of a Romani family whose home was firebombed on March 14, 2010. The two neighbours were charged with attempted murder. The Romea article Czech Republic: Yet another arson attack on a Romani home18 reports that a Molotov cocktail was thrown into a house on railway property occupied by a Romani Family in Krty, Czech Republic and one man suffered second-degree burns as a result of the attack. Also reported is that firefighters from Jesenice, Knezeves, and Rakovnik were on the scene immediately, as was a railway firefighting unit from Plzen and the burn victim was taken to hospital in Rakovnik for treatment of the burns on his leg. It is further reported that police are investigating the case as one of attempted grievous bodily harm for which the perpetrators would face between five and 12 years in prison.

Although many of the reports and articles contained in counsel's documentary evidence describe the problems of the Roma in the Czech Republic, accounts of the Czech Republic's efforts and successes in providing better protection for the Roma are often contained in the same reports and articles. This reflects the Czech Republic's commitment to address the problems encountered by the Roma and eradicate violence and discrimination against this group.

In summary, I find that the preponderance of the documentary evidence indicates that the Czech Republic is making very serious efforts to provide better protection to the Roma, whether as victims of hate crimes to assistance in obtaining social services or inclusion into Czech society. While there is discrimination against Roma people and even some incidents of violence, I find that the Czech Republic government, in recent years, is making very serious strides to have this discrimination overcome. I also find that the Czech Republic government has been successful in its endeavors to provide effective state protection to all its citizens, including the Roma.

There is no persuasive evidence before me that the claimants would face persecution or, on a balance of probabilities, face a risk to their life or to cruel and unusual treatment or punishment or to a danger of torture, if they returned to the Czech Republic. For all these reasons, I find that the claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection, whether under section 96 or section 97 of the Act, as state protection is available to them.

As the claims of the minor children rely entirely on the evidence of their parents, and no persuasive evidence was adduced to differentiate their claims from those of their parents, their claims must also fail.

For all these reasons, the claims are rejected. The claimants are not Convention refugees or persons in need of protection. (signed) "M. Pettinella" M.
